page.title: Docs Site Decisions
page.lede: Three invented decisions about a documentation site, to show the format. Read top down: [[41]] sets the direction for the rest.

A stale cache is a leftover copy of an old build that the laptop reused by mistake: it broke two publishes this month, and clearing it once ([[38]]) held for a week. The docs site is built and published from one maintainer's laptop today; CI is the shared build service that runs on every merge to `main`. A stale cache is a leftover copy of an old build that the laptop reused by mistake: it broke two publishes this month, and clearing it once ([[38]], answered: clear it) held for a week. CI already builds the site on every merge as a check, then throws the result away; publishing from it adds one deploy step, the same command the maintainer runs by hand, and one secret, the deploy token. The maintainer is away from the 20th for two weeks, and until the build moves nobody else can publish. You decide where the build runs from now on; [[42]] and [[43]] arise only if it moves.

why: Two publishes broke this month, both from the laptop's stale cache; clearing it once ([[38]]) held for a week. The maintainer is away from the 20th. Blocks [[42]] and [[43]].

Two publishes broke this month, both from the laptop's stale cache; clearing it once ([[38]]) held for a week. The maintainer who publishes is away from the 20th for two weeks, and nobody else can publish while the build lives on that laptop. Blocks [[42]] and [[43]], which arise only if the build moves.
whyask: Moving the build changes who can publish: from CI, every merge to `main` goes live within minutes, so a change can no longer be held back after merging.

Moving the build changes who can publish. Today one person publishes by hand, when they choose; from CI, every merge to `main` goes live within minutes. If the team relies on holding a change back after merging (a release-day page, say), that habit breaks, and the repo does not show whether it does.
evidence: Observed: both failed publishes reused the same stale `.cache/build` directory; CI's builds of the same commits passed (`https://ci.example.com/docs-site/builds`).
Inferred: CI publishes would not hit the cache failure, since every CI build starts clean.

Observed: the build logs of both failed publishes show the same stale `.cache/build` directory, reused from an older build; CI's check builds of the same commits passed (`https://ci.example.com/docs-site/builds`).
Observed: CI already runs the full build on every merge, in about 4 minutes (the same builds page).
Inferred: CI publishes would not hit the cache failure, since every CI build starts from a clean checkout.
Observed: the deploy step CI would need is the same command the maintainer runs by hand (`scripts/publish.sh`); it reads the deploy token from the environment, so CI needs only the secret.
Assumed: nobody publishes from a fork; the repo settings do not show it either way, and no fork has opened a docs change this year.

a: Keep building on the maintainer's laptop and publishing by hand. The stale-cache failures stay at about two a month.

Keep building on the maintainer's laptop. Nothing changes: they build, check the preview and publish by hand when they choose. The stale-cache failures stay at about two a month, each found when a reader reports a broken page and fixed by clearing the cache and publishing again.
b: Build and publish from CI on every merge to `main`; the laptop build stays for previews. Each merge publishes within about 4 minutes.

Build and publish from CI on every merge to `main`; the laptop build stays for previews only. The first CI publish replaces the live site, and each later merge publishes within about 4 minutes. Publishing no longer waits for one person, and a failed build stops the publish instead of shipping a broken page.

tldr: The CI build changes some page URLs
Redirect them, or let them break
cards.context: Building in CI ([[41]], option b) gives twelve pages a new web address (URL): the ten how-to guides and the two pages that list the site's configuration options, all of which move under a new /docs/ folder. A redirect is one config line that sends a reader from an old URL to its new one. Only matters if [[41]] is (b). You decide what happens to links that point at the old addresses.
cards.why: Needed before the first CI publish. Blocks nothing else.
cards.whyask: Breaking public links is a call about readers, not about the build.
o: Add a redirect for each of the twelve URLs.
Old links keep working; twelve lines of redirect config to maintain.
Let the old URLs return not found.
External links break; search ranking for those pages is lost and cannot be won back on demand.

a.undo: Remove the redirect lines; nothing else changes.

b.undo: Cannot be fully undone: once search engines drop the old URLs, redirects added later do not win the ranking back.

You decide what happens to links that point at the old addresses.

why: Needed before the first CI publish, which moves the twelve pages and breaks their old addresses unless the redirects are already in the config.

Needed before the first CI publish: that publish moves the twelve pages, and their old addresses break the moment it goes live unless the redirects are already in the config. Nothing else waits on it. If [[41]] is (a), the pages do not move and this card no longer applies.
whyask: Breaking public links is a call about readers, not about the build: other sites and bookmarks point at these pages, and a lost link cannot be won back.

Breaking public links is a call about readers, not about the build. Other sites, old forum answers and bookmarks point at these pages; whether those readers are worth twelve config lines is a judgement about the audience, and a lost link cannot be won back later.
evidence: Observed: the trial CI build lists the twelve pages whose paths change (`build/moved-pages.txt` from that run). Estimated: about a fifth of the visits to those pages arrive from other sites, from last month's referrer report (`https://analytics.example.com/docs-site/referrers`).

Observed: the trial CI build lists the twelve pages whose paths change (`build/moved-pages.txt` from that run). Estimated: about a fifth of the visits to those pages arrive from other sites, read from last month's referrer report (`https://analytics.example.com/docs-site/referrers`). Unknown: how many sites link to them; the report counts visits, not links. Observed: the site generator reads redirects from its config file, one line each (`https://docs.example.com/generator/redirects`). Assumed: those redirects work as its documentation says; not tried here, and the first CI publish would show it.

a: Add a redirect for each of the twelve old URLs before the first CI publish, one line per page in the site config.

Add a redirect for each of the twelve old URLs before the first CI publish, one line per page in the site config. A reader following an old link lands on the new page without noticing. The twelve lines stay in the config, and need changing only if those pages move again.
b: Let the twelve old URLs return not found from the first CI publish; a reader following an old link sees an error page.

Let the twelve old URLs return not found from the first CI publish. A reader following an old link sees an error page and has to search for the new one. Search engines drop the old addresses within weeks, and redirects added after that do not win the ranking back.

impact.effect: (a) no visual change; (b) the site matches the logo
impact.wait: the site keeps the blue meanwhile

tldr: The CI build can apply a new theme
Pick a colour, or keep the current one
cards.context: Building in CI ([[41]], option b) applies the site's theme afresh, so the accent colour (the colour of links and headings) can change at no extra cost. The site is blue today; the logo is green. Either colour is one theme setting, a single line in the site's theme file, so it is easy to change back. You pick which the site uses.
cards.why: Nothing forces it. It is raised because the move to CI rebuilds the theme from its source files, so a change made now costs nothing extra; made later, it is a separate theme build and a check of every page's contrast.
cards.whyask: A taste call: no fact settles it. The blue has been the site's colour since launch, and readers know it; the green matches the logo and the product's other sites. Both read well in the light and dark themes (checked), so the choice is only how the site should look.
o: Keep the current blue for links and headings. Nothing changes for readers, and the screenshots in the guides stay accurate. The site stays a different colour from the logo, as it has been since launch.

Switch links and headings to the logo's green at the first CI publish. The site matches the logo and the product's other sites. The screenshots in the guides still show the blue until they are retaken, which reads as dated to a careful reader.
The site matches the logo; screenshots in the guides look dated until refreshed.
The site keeps the blue meanwhile.

a.happens: No visual change; the site stays blue.

b.happens: Links and headings turn the logo's green from the first CI publish.
b.undo: One theme setting: change it back in one line.
b.who: Readers of the docs site, and the guide screenshots.
b.cost: The guide screenshots look dated until they are retaken, about an hour.

cards.evidence: Checked: nothing in the site's build or its pages reads the accent colour except the theme file, so a change is one line there (`theme/colors.toml`). Checked: both colours pass the contrast check against the light and the dark background. Not checked: what readers prefer; no survey of them exists.
